Check the licence: some leading tabular models restrict commercial use. Public benchmark gains may not transfer to enterprise data that changes over time.
entries.where: Small or medium structured datasets where rapid experimentation helps.
entries.test: Time-aware or grouped holdouts; calibration, compute and maintainability compared.
entries.failure: Benchmark gains that vanish on changing enterprise data, or a licence that forbids your use.

entries.title: Time-series foundation models
entries.summary: Pretrained forecasting models can produce useful forecasts with little tuning.
judgement: Pretrained forecasting models can produce useful forecasts with little tuning [178]. Evaluate them beside seasonal and statistical baselines at the horizon the decision actually needs, with rolling-origin tests that respect time. Examine prediction intervals, covariates and regime shifts. A good average forecast can miss the peaks that determine capacity, so score the peaks.
entries.where: Demand, staffing, inventory or asset signals with a usable history.
entries.test: Rolling-origin tests; covariates, intervals and regime shifts examined.
entries.failure: A good average forecast that misses the capacity peaks.

entries.title: Causal inference and experiments
entries.summary: Many decisions ask what happens if the organisation acts differently: a new price, a new process, a new staffing rule.
judgement: Many decisions ask what happens if the organisation acts differently: a new price, a new process, a new staffing rule. Predictive accuracy alone does not establish the effect of an intervention. State the causal model and its assumptions, examine confounding, and run sensitivity and refutation checks, or run a randomised experiment where you can [185]. The same discipline applies to claims about AI's own effect on productivity (IR-084).
entries.where: Decisions about the effect of acting differently.
entries.test: State the causal model; examine confounding; run sensitivity or refutation checks.
entries.failure: Predictive accuracy read as a treatment effect.

entries.title: Optimisation and constraint solvers
entries.summary: Rosters, routes, allocations and schedules are optimisation problems with defined objectives and hard limits.
judgement: Rosters, routes, allocations and schedules are optimisation problems with defined objectives and hard limits. A suitable solver searches for feasible plans and may prove optimality or infeasibility; a timeout can leave the answer unresolved. In a combined system, a language model helps people state the problem and read the answer [173]. Asking a language model to produce the plan directly invites infeasible or unstable results. A mathematically optimal plan can still optimise an incomplete objective, so test operational acceptance with the people who run the work.
entries.where: Rosters, routing, allocation or scheduling with defined objectives and limits.
entries.test: Feasibility, objective trade-offs, infeasible inputs and operational acceptance.
entries.failure: An optimal plan for an incomplete objective.
entries.examples: OR-Tools; CP-SAT; routing and scheduling solvers.

entries.title: Computer vision for inspection
entries.summary: Bounded visual tasks (a defect on a line, a missing label, a damaged part) suit task-specific vision models trained on representative images, with a reviewed process for exceptions.
judgement: Bounded visual tasks (a defect on a line, a missing label, a damaged part) suit task-specific vision models trained on representative images, with a reviewed process for exceptions. Test on the real line: lighting, camera changes, rare faults and the cost of a missed defect. A demonstration under ideal lighting falls short of a validated inspection system, and regulated manufacturing calls for that validation.
entries.where: Bounded defect or detection tasks in manufacturing or operations.
entries.test: Lighting, camera changes, rare faults and false-negative costs on the real line.
entries.failure: A demonstration mistaken for a validated system.
entries.examples: Detection; segmentation; vision encoders; inspection benchmarks such as MVTec AD [201].

entries.title: Graph analytics and relational prediction
entries.summary: Fraud rings, supply-chain exposure and asset dependencies live in relationships that row-level prediction misses.
judgement: Fraud rings, supply-chain exposure and asset dependencies live in relationships that row-level prediction misses. Graph queries and graph models represent them explicitly. They also bring their own hazards: entity resolution errors, leakage across connected train and test splits, and bias that spreads along the edges. Evaluate on a decision where the relationships clearly matter.
entries.where: Fraud, supply-chain or asset decisions that depend on connected entities.
entries.test: Entity resolution, leakage across connected splits and explanation fidelity.
entries.failure: Bias and spurious associations that spread through the graph.
entries.examples: Graph queries; graph neural networks; standardised graph benchmarks and splits [202].

entries.title: Simulation and digital twins
entries.summary: A calibrated model of a process lets people examine scenarios that would be costly or hazardous to try directly, and it gives agents a safe place to rehearse.
judgement: A calibrated model of a process lets people examine scenarios that would be costly or hazardous to try directly, and it gives agents a safe place to rehearse. A detailed simulation can also create confidence beyond its validated range. Keep calibration and assumptions visible, and compare simulated with observed behaviour across the range you intend to use.
entries.where: Changes that are costly or hazardous to test directly.
entries.test: Simulated against observed behaviour over the intended operating range.
entries.failure: Confidence that extends beyond the validated range.
entries.examples: Process simulators; calibrated digital twins; the ISO 23247 digital twin framework for manufacturing [203].

entries.title: Scientific discovery with AI
entries.summary: AI-assisted discovery moved fast in the second half of 2026.
judgement: AI-assisted discovery moved fast in the second half of 2026. About a quarter of August's mathematics submissions to arXiv disclosed AI use [25]; researchers directing agents proved the 31-year-old KLS conjecture in a preprint, and further proofs by other groups followed [26]; OpenAI released 722 manuscripts at once and withdrew 3 the next day [27]; competing refutations of the Exponential Time Hypothesis await examination [28]. Results in biology arrived with careful limits and contested credit [90, 91]. Ask two questions of any claim: who contributed to each step, and how thoroughly the result has been verified. The enterprise posture is Plan for: research organisations need review capacity for a growing volume of candidate results.
entries.where: Domains where experts can verify a result by independent methods.
entries.test: Audit the chain from generated hypothesis to proof, experiment or replication.
entries.failure: Candidate findings that overwhelm verification capacity.
entries.examples: Human-directed agentic search; proof and experiment pipelines.

entries.title: Edge inference and on-device AI
entries.summary: Run inference near the work when latency, connectivity, privacy or token cost makes a measurable difference: a factory floor, a vehicle, a clinic with poor connectivity, a developer's laptop.
judgement: Run inference near the work when latency, connectivity, privacy or token cost makes a measurable difference: a factory floor, a vehicle, a clinic with poor connectivity, a developer's laptop. Local inference now reaches well beyond phones. On a laptop with 128 GB of memory, The Register measured a 35-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model at 67.6 tokens a second; the graphics processor passed 90°C within an hour of sustained load, and the reviewer judged the cost case weak so far [244]. Platforms now let teams route each task to the device or the cloud: Windows ML runs llama.cpp across graphics, neural and central processors, and Google added structured output and early agent interfaces to its on-device Gemini Nano [239, 245]. An aggregate open-weight benchmark result [207] does not establish that a model will fit a particular device.

Running locally keeps model, update and device risks in place, and it does not by itself keep data private: in tests reported in October, a model promoted for local use tried, in fewer than one call in 100,000, to send a file to a cloud storage bucket abroad [246]. Treat local models as untrusted code, with containment, egress rules and monitoring (IR-034), and test thermal limits, updates, offline failure and local data exposure. The enterprise posture is Test because the tools shipped in the second half of 2026 and the cost case needs proving on your own work.
entries.where: Bounded tasks that must continue under limited network access, or that handle data the organisation prefers to keep on the device.
entries.test: Thermal limits, updates, offline failure, local data exposure and outbound connections, with cost per accepted task against the cloud.
entries.failure: Devices that drift out of date, overheat under sustained load or send data out unnoticed.
entries.examples: Small and mixture-of-experts models; edge accelerators; Windows ML, Apple Core AI and Gemini Nano; llama.cpp.

entries.title: Robotics and vision-language-action systems
entries.summary: Models that turn vision and language into physical action are improving, and deployments of conventional robots keep growing: the operational stock of industrial robots reached a record in 2025, and robotaxi services expanded.
judgement: Models that turn vision and language into physical action are improving, and deployments of conventional robots keep growing: the operational stock of industrial robots reached a record in 2025 [107], and robotaxi services expanded [106]. Study physical autonomy through bounded demonstrations on a specific manipulation or movement task, with competent safety engineering. A general demonstration is weak evidence of safe operation in your workplace.
entries.where: A specific manipulation or movement task that warrants investment.
entries.test: Failure recovery, human takeover and transfer from simulation to real conditions.
entries.failure: A general demonstration read as evidence of safety in your setting.

entries.title: Unconstrained physical autonomy
entries.summary: Keep open-world physical action out of deployment until the safety case matches the operating environment.
judgement: Keep open-world physical action out of deployment until the safety case matches the operating environment. People, equipment and materials can be harmed by unbounded action, and physical harm cannot be undone like a software change. Require domain-specific validation, safe stops and independent incident review before deployment.
entries.where: Settings where unbounded action could harm people, equipment or materials.
entries.test: Domain-specific validation, safe stops and independent incident review.
entries.failure: A software-style release process applied to physical risk.

entries.title: Document drafting and analysis assistants
entries.summary: Begin with reviewable work where the user can judge both the content and the evidence: drafting, summarising, comparing and checking documents.
judgement: Begin with reviewable work where the user can judge both the content and the evidence: drafting, summarising, comparing and checking documents. Staff keep responsibility and need access to the original sources. Faster first drafts can increase verification time, so measure the accepted final document, the review effort and the severity of errors against the baseline, and count the hours spent checking.
entries.where: Staff who retain responsibility and can see the original sources.
entries.test: Final accepted documents, review effort and error severity against the baseline.
entries.failure: Faster drafts that cost more time to verify.

entries.title: Customer-service copilots
entries.summary: Support service staff with grounded retrieval and draft responses before giving any system authority over transactions.
judgement: Support service staff with grounded retrieval and draft responses before giving any system authority over transactions. A service team with known policies, escalation paths and quality measures can test this safely. In a study of 5,179 customer-support agents published in 2023, an assistant raised issues resolved per hour by 14% on average and by 34% for novice workers [204]. Response speed can improve while the customer outcome worsens, so track resolution, repeat contact, customer harm and the effort staff spend correcting drafts.
entries.where: Service teams with known policies, escalation paths and quality measures.
entries.test: Resolution, repeat contact, customer harm and correction effort.
entries.failure: Faster responses with worse outcomes.

entries.title: Contact-centre automation
entries.summary: Fully automated handling suits clearly bounded intents with reliable escalation, and the organisation must be able to monitor complete journeys.
judgement: Fully automated handling suits clearly bounded intents with reliable escalation, and the organisation must be able to monitor complete journeys. Deflection rates can disguise abandonment and unresolved problems. New York City proposed rules in the second half of 2026 that would require an easy route to a person in AI customer service [116]. The enterprise posture is Revisit for organisations that set deflection targets without measuring the journey's outcome.
entries.where: Organisations that can monitor complete journeys, beyond call deflection.
entries.test: Failed handoffs, repeat contacts, accessibility and complaint outcomes.
entries.failure: Deflection that disguises abandonment.

entries.title: Enterprise search and knowledge assistance
entries.summary: Offer answers grounded in evidence, with permissions applied and uncertainty visible.
judgement: Offer answers grounded in evidence, with permissions applied and uncertainty visible. Knowledge in most organisations is dispersed, and the owners of each source should be identifiable before an assistant answers on their behalf. A polished interface can mask poor information underneath; measure useful answers, unsupported answers and the time to a correct decision. Build on permission-aware, hybrid retrieval (IR-013, IR-014).
entries.where: Dispersed knowledge with identifiable owners.
entries.test: Useful answers, unsupported answers and time to a correct decision.
entries.failure: A polished interface over poor information.

entries.title: Process mining before automation
entries.summary: Map the actual work, its exceptions and its handoffs before deciding what to delegate.
judgement: Map the actual work, its exceptions and its handoffs before deciding what to delegate. Teams often disagree about the real process, and a formal process map may omit the actual bottleneck. Event logs help [205], but they omit the informal work that keeps a process running, so validate the data with the staff who do the work and compare the proposed process with real cases.
entries.where: Teams that disagree about the real process or its bottlenecks.
entries.test: Validate event data with staff; compare the proposed process with actual cases.
entries.failure: A log that misses the informal work holding the process together.

entries.title: Expert workflows and decision support
entries.summary: In expert work, the assistant's job is to bring the evidence and conditions behind a decision into view and to keep disagreement visible, while the decision stays with the expert.
judgement: In expert work, the assistant's job is to bring the evidence and conditions behind a decision into view and to keep disagreement visible, while the decision stays with the expert. Strong diagnostic results reported in the second half of 2026 still await clinical testing [92], and few cleared medical AI devices have measured patient outcomes [94]. A system can also standardise a mistaken or local expert habit. Compare decision quality, escalation and explanation across experience levels.
entries.where: Experienced staff who can adjudicate cases and define a safe scope.
entries.test: Decision quality, escalation and explanation across experience levels.
entries.failure: A system that spreads one expert's mistaken habit.

entries.title: Creative and synthetic media workflows
entries.summary: Generated images, audio and video can serve marketing, training and communication within explicit rights, provenance and editorial review.
judgement: Generated images, audio and video can serve marketing, training and communication within explicit rights, provenance and editorial review. Convincing media can mislead viewers or hide its origin. New EU AI Act transparency requirements began to apply on 2 August 2026 [49]; check which apply to your system and role (IR-092). The enterprise posture is Revisit for organisations that publish generated media without disclosure or a responsible publisher.
entries.where: Work with a responsible publisher and a clear intended audience.
entries.test: Factual representation, permissions, brand fit, accessibility and disclosure before release.
entries.failure: Convincing media that misleads or hides its origin.

entries.title: Human learning and apprenticeship
entries.summary: Redesign junior work so that assistance preserves the practice people need to become experts.
judgement: Redesign junior work so that assistance preserves the practice people need to become experts. Stanford's payroll study puts employment of 22 to 25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed occupations 19% below a comparison path, mainly through weaker hiring, though the estimate loses significance with all controls and Yale's Budget Lab finds no clear aggregate effect [77, 78]; inside Anthropic, junior technical hires fell from 27% to 9% of technical hiring [79]. Short-term output gains can weaken the pipeline of future reviewers, and verification depends on experienced people. Measure unaided competence and supervision load alongside throughput.
entries.where: Roles where AI changes the tasks through which people used to learn.
entries.test: Unaided competence and supervision load alongside throughput.
entries.failure: Short-term output gains that weaken the future pool of reviewers.
entries.examples: Practice tasks; supervised rotations; capability assessments.

entries.title: AI literacy and supported adoption
entries.summary: Give staff practical training, permitted tools and a way to report failures and propose improvements.
judgement: Give staff practical training, permitted tools and a way to report failures and propose improvements. Use is often uneven and informal: 31% of UK workers who use generative AI do so without their employer's knowledge [75]. Observe real task choices and support needs; course attendance alone tells you little. The enterprise posture is Revisit for organisations whose policy rests on prohibition alone.
entries.where: Organisations where use is uneven or informal tools already shape work.
entries.test: Real task choices and support needs, observed in the work.
entries.failure: Training without workflow support.
entries.examples: Role-specific learning; adoption support; an authorised route for staff.

entries.title: Accessible and multilingual AI services
entries.summary: Test a service with the people and languages it must serve, including people who use assistive technology and people who need the service in a minority language.
judgement: Test a service with the people and languages it must serve, including people who use assistive technology and people who need the service in a minority language. For Irish services, test Irish-language provision where relevant, alongside regional accents and other languages users need. Aggregate quality can conceal exclusion for a smaller group, and public opinion on AI in services varies with the stakes: patients in one survey were comfortable with AI scribes for routine checks (48%) far more than for discussions of domestic abuse (23%) [108]. Keep a workable route for people who cannot or will not use the AI service.
entries.where: Public or customer services with diverse users and accessibility needs.
entries.test: Task completion with assistive technologies and each relevant language group.
entries.failure: Good average quality that hides exclusion.
entries.examples: Tests in every language the service offers; accessible interfaces; non-AI alternatives.

entries.title: Agent commerce and delegated purchasing
entries.summary: Platforms split in the second half of 2026 over whether to let agents shop.
judgement: Platforms split in the second half of 2026 over whether to let agents shop. Amazon blocked Meta's Muse from shopping on its site [105]; Walmart opened a gateway for agents with spending limits and a returns guarantee "including when an agent doesn't act as intended" [102]; American Express admits customer agents only through approved channels [104]; two protocols compete [103, 161]. Explore purchasing agents only with clear limits, consent, reversibility and dispute handling. Wait on consumer personal agents with access to staff financial or corporate accounts until access controls and liability terms settle.
entries.where: A bounded purchase journey that can tolerate supervised testing.
entries.test: Incorrect orders, duplicate payments, refunds and authority limits.
entries.failure: Unclear responsibility for a loss.

entries.title: Organisation-wide productivity claims
entries.summary: Withhold broad claims of return on investment until outcomes, full costs and comparison periods are credible.
judgement: Withhold broad claims of return on investment until outcomes, full costs and comparison periods are credible. Surveys published in the first half of 2026 showed modest realised savings (nearly 40% of the firms in Bain's survey that measured savings realised 10% or less) and little change in employment [62, 83]. Activity and self-reported time saved are easily mistaken for value. Separate measured outcomes, reported savings and forecasts, and look for displaced work. The enterprise posture is Revisit for any business case that extrapolates from demonstrations, surveys or isolated wins.
entries.where: Business cases that extrapolate from demonstrations, surveys or isolated wins.
entries.test: Separate measured outcomes, reported savings and forecasts, including displacement.
entries.failure: Activity and self-reported time saved presented as realised value.
entries.examples: Outcome studies; controlled or carefully matched comparisons.

entries.title: AI service and dependency inventory
entries.summary: Know which models, tools, data flows and owners support each production capability.
judgement: Know which models, tools, data flows and owners support each production capability. AI now sits inside products, teams and suppliers, and some of it arrives unannounced: 31% of UK workers who use generative AI do so without their employer's knowledge [75]. Shadow integrations escape change control and incident response. Trace one business outcome to every dependency and name the accountable owner. The enterprise posture is Revisit because, in Brightbeam's experience, most inventories list applications and miss the models and tools inside them.
entries.where: AI embedded in several products, teams or suppliers.
entries.test: Trace one business outcome to every dependency and its accountable owner.
entries.failure: Shadow integrations outside change control.

entries.title: Observability with purposeful traces
entries.summary: Connect task outcomes, tool actions and failures so a team can diagnose problems across model and tool boundaries.
judgement: Connect task outcomes, tool actions and failures so a team can diagnose problems across model and tool boundaries. Collect with a purpose: traces of everything create cost and a second sensitive dataset without improving diagnosis [193]. Open conventions for tracing generative AI are emerging [169], and evaluation platforms record traces alongside results [184]. Reconstruct a real incident from the traces, and check redaction, retention and permissions as you do.
entries.where: Teams that diagnose failures across model and tool boundaries.
entries.test: Reconstruct an incident; verify redaction, retention and permissions.
entries.failure: Traces that cost more than they explain.

entries.title: Evaluation-gated releases and model retirement
entries.summary: Treat every model change as a release, with regression tests and an exit path.
judgement: Treat every model change as a release, with regression tests and an exit path. Nine major model releases arrived between 3 September and 26 October 2026 [15, 68, 69, 122, 123, 128 to 131], and hosted models can be changed or retired; in Brightbeam's experience, notice periods range from about 60 days to 12 months, and providers publish their schedules [188 to 192]. A compatible API can hide materially different behaviour. Keep prompts, harnesses and evaluations under version control, run the regression suite against each successor model, and rehearse the migration before a notice arrives.
entries.where: Hosted models or dependencies that can change or be retired.
entries.test: Rehearse a migration with realistic notice and an accepted fallback.
entries.failure: A compatible API with different behaviour.

entries.title: Cost per accepted task and FinOps
entries.summary: Budget the whole system and report cost against accepted work.
judgement: Budget the whole system and report cost against accepted work. Cost per accepted task is the allocated cost of compute, tools, review, rework and operations for all attempts in a defined task cohort, divided by the unique tasks accepted from that cohort; report rejected, abandoned and escalated tasks beside it, and note that the ratio is undefined when no tasks are accepted. Use consistent allocation rules, state how setup costs and delayed acceptance are treated, and compare like tasks at the same quality threshold. Cheap tokens can sit inside an expensive workflow: token prices fell steeply in the second half of 2026 while some costs per task rose [23, 66, 67], and pricing moved towards consumption and outcomes [70, 126].
entries.where: Growing usage, or pricing that shifts from seats to consumption.
entries.test: Include idle capacity, retries, review, rework, support and failed tasks.
entries.failure: Cheap tokens inside an expensive workflow.

entries.title: Rate limits, queues and spend controls
entries.summary: Bound concurrency, retries and spending at the system boundary.
judgement: Bound concurrency, retries and spending at the system boundary. Agents can loop, burst and nest tool calls, and OWASP lists unbounded consumption among the top risks for LLM applications [170]. A budget alarm that fires after the event can arrive too late. Usage-based billing spread from June 2026, from coding tools to enterprise platforms [70, 126], and one provider's introductory price doubles after 30 November 2026 [69]. Set caps per job profile, test runaway and outage scenarios, and make the service degrade gracefully.
entries.where: Agents that can generate loops, bursts or nested tool calls.
entries.test: Runaway and outage scenarios; verify limits and graceful degradation.
entries.failure: An alarm that arrives after the money is spent.
entries.examples: Token and spend caps; backpressure; circuit breakers.

entries.title: Resilience and supplier exit
entries.summary: Test continuity in case a model, cloud region, tool provider or contract becomes unavailable.
judgement: Test continuity in case a model, cloud region, tool provider or contract becomes unavailable. In the second half of 2026 a laboratory withheld a model [5], another disclosed a training pause of more than a month [37], and a GPU cloud's bonds traded at 81 cents on the dollar [33]. Several vendors can still depend on the same underlying infrastructure. Map who backs your provider's capacity, keep exit and assignment rights, and exercise fallback, degraded service and data export against a real time budget.
entries.where: Processes where a supplier outage matters.
entries.test: Exercise fallback, degraded service and data export with a real time budget.
entries.failure: Several suppliers that share one point of failure.
entries.examples: Exit plans; fallback models; portable records.

entries.title: Sovereignty beyond data residency
entries.summary: Where processing happens is one part of control.
judgement: Where processing happens is one part of control. Support access, key management, subprocessors, portability and the ability to operate independently matter as much, and data location alone leaves open whose courts can compel access: the US CLOUD Act, for example, clarifies that qualifying legal process can reach data in a covered provider's possession, custody or control, including data stored abroad [206]. Map them for each critical service. The enterprise posture is Revisit because many sovereignty decisions still stop at the hosting region.
entries.where: Architecture choices shaped by jurisdiction, strategic dependency or sensitive data.
entries.test: Map support access, keys, subprocessors, portability and independent operation.
entries.failure: Local hosting mistaken for control.
entries.examples: Control assessments; hosting and key-management options.

entries.title: EU and national regulatory readiness
entries.summary: Keep an obligations map for each use case, with qualified review and dated evidence.
judgement: Keep an obligations map for each use case, with qualified review and dated evidence. On 9 October 2026 the Commission said the EU AI Office had sent its first formal requests to frontier providers [12]; EN 18286 was cited in the Official Journal on 14 October 2026 [50]; high-risk obligations apply from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) and 2 August 2028 (Annex I products) [49]. Member states are adding national measures: in Ireland, the Regulation of Artificial Intelligence Act 2026 created the AI Office of Ireland [55], and court directions now govern AI-assisted documents [54]. A generic AI Act date applied to the wrong system or role misleads, so check the intended purpose, the roles and the actual timetable.
entries.where: Systems that enter a regulated or public-service process.
entries.test: Intended purpose, roles, applicable rules and the actual timetable.
entries.failure: A generic date applied to the wrong system or role.
entries.examples: System inventories; legal and quality review.

entries.title: Validated change in regulated operations
entries.summary: Where quality, safety or model-risk systems already govern a process, separate the stable controls from the model components that change, and define the evidence each kind of change needs.
judgement: Where quality, safety or model-risk systems already govern a process, separate the stable controls from the model components that change, and define the evidence each kind of change needs. A component remains subject to validation even when it is designed to be replaced. Classify a model update, demonstrate repeatable acceptance and rollback, and agree the classification with quality and compliance before the first update arrives.
entries.where: Processes already governed by quality, safety or model-risk systems.
entries.test: Classify a model update; demonstrate repeatable acceptance and rollback.
entries.failure: Replaceable components treated as exempt from validation.

entries.title: Compute capacity, energy and location
entries.summary: Plan infrastructure around measured demand, availability and local constraints.
judgement: Plan infrastructure around measured demand, availability and local constraints. In the United States, a capacity auction cleared short of its reliability requirement [43]. Oracle served a force majeure notice on a Stargate campus in New Mexico after state officials refused rights of way for its gas supply [231]. In Ireland, data centres used about 23% of metered electricity in 2025, and new data centres of 10 MVA or more must now bring matching dispatchable generation or storage [44, 45]; most adults there want building stopped for now [46]. Data-centre electricity figures include demand unrelated to AI. Treat permission, power and community terms as delivery risks with their own timelines when choosing regions and providers.
entries.where: Plans for dedicated capacity or a large inference workload.
entries.test: Utilisation, power assumptions, grid dependencies and alternatives.
entries.failure: Capacity plans that ignore permission and grid timelines.

entries.title: National outcome evidence and sector benchmarks
entries.summary: Official statistics in the US, the EU and Ireland count the enterprises that use AI; no public series the editors found measures what work AI completes, whether that work is accepted and what it costs.
judgement: Official statistics in the US, the EU and Ireland count the enterprises that use AI [72, 74, 186]; no public series the editors found measures what work AI completes, whether that work is accepted and what it costs. Build that evidence with shared definitions, protected data and independent review: sector case panels that publish denominators, sample selection, failure rates and accepted-work costs. National adoption programmes and regulators' supervisory experience provide a foundation for this work [56, 112]. Convenience samples can be mistaken for national performance.
entries.where: Partners who can contribute representative operational cases.
entries.test: Publish denominators, sample selection, failure rates and accepted-work costs.
entries.failure: Convenience samples presented as national performance.
entries.examples: National adoption statistics; proposed sector case panels.

entries.title: Continuous operation of AI systems
entries.summary: Deployed intelligence needs a standing cycle of observation, evaluation, authorised change and learning, with owners for quality, cost, incidents, knowledge updates and model changes.
judgement: Deployed intelligence needs a standing cycle of observation, evaluation, authorised change and learning, with owners for quality, cost, incidents, knowledge updates and model changes. Systems drift, and feedback fades after the pilot. A new operating label achieves little without capacity and accountability.
entries.where: AI that is becoming part of ordinary operational work.
entries.test: Assign owners for quality, cost, incidents, knowledge updates and model changes.
entries.failure: A new label with no capacity behind it.
entries.examples: Operational review cycles; named owners for quality, cost, incidents and model changes.

entries.title: Accelerators beyond a single vendor
entries.summary: Prove a second accelerator family on your own workloads before you rely on it.
judgement: Prove a second accelerator family on your own workloads before you rely on it. Running inference beyond a single vendor's platform became practical in the second half of 2026: Alphabet named sales of TPU systems as a meaningful contributor to Google Cloud's 103% revenue growth [208], AMD put its Helios racks into production, with OpenAI bringing them online from the fourth quarter and Anthropic planning up to 2 GW [209], and native PyTorch backends for Google's TPUs and AWS Trainium shipped in October; the Trainium backend, a public beta, still skips about 22,000 PyTorch tests [210, 211].

Measured results vary by model, precision and serving software. SemiAnalysis measured TPUv7 at up to 50% better performance per dollar than Nvidia's B200 and B300 when serving one large model at FP8, while Nvidia kept the lead at FP4 and was up to five times more cost-efficient than AMD on one agentic coding benchmark [212, 213]. Much of AMD's new capacity arrives from the fourth quarter of 2026 into 2027 [209]. Keep serving code on portable layers, benchmark one production workload on a second accelerator through a cloud, and ask for second-source options in 2027 capacity contracts. The enterprise posture is Test because the gap between platforms depends on your model and your serving engine as much as on the chip.
entries.where: Inference large enough that price per token, supply or dependence on one vendor matters, on open-weight or portable models.
entries.test: Accuracy and cost per accepted task for one production workload on each candidate accelerator, with the same model, precision and serving engine.
entries.failure: A headline benchmark that matches neither your model, your precision nor your serving engine.
entries.examples: Google TPU (Ironwood); AWS Trainium; AMD Instinct and Helios; Microsoft Maia; PyTorch, vLLM and SGLang; TorchTPU and TorchNeuron.

entries.title: Inference-specialised hardware
entries.summary: Buy speed as a service, and check accuracy on your own tasks.
judgement: Buy speed as a service, and check accuracy on your own tasks. Chips built for inference now generate tokens markedly faster for some open models, which matters for coding agents, voice and other work where people wait. Nvidia put its Groq 3 LPX into full production, citing 3,400 output tokens a second on one 31-billion-parameter model [215]; that result needs at least 64 of its chips, against one or two of Cerebras's wafer-scale processors for the same model [216]. Cerebras's cloud revenue nearly quadrupled on a year earlier, at a gross margin of 14% [217]. Independent benchmarks barely cover the field: the latest MLPerf inference round drew a record 30 submitters, none of them Cerebras, Groq or SambaNova [214].

Speed and accuracy can diverge at the endpoint: Artificial Analysis found the same open-weight model scoring 22% on a tool-calling test at some providers, against 37% for the reference [218]. The field is consolidating into the largest chip makers, and some vendors depend on a few customers and fresh capital: Nvidia licensed Groq's technology, AMD agreed to buy Taalas, and Groq raised money twice in under three months [216, 219, 220]. Pilot latency-bound work through APIs, and avoid hardware purchases or long prepaid commitments with these vendors for now. The enterprise posture is Test because the gain is real for some work and needs proving on yours.
entries.where: Latency-bound work, such as coding agents, voice and interactive search, on the open-weight models these services support.
entries.test: Speed, accuracy against a reference endpoint and cost per accepted task on your own prompts, measured through each provider's API.
entries.failure: A fast endpoint that loses accuracy through its serving settings, or a supplier that fails during a prepaid contract.
entries.examples: Groq 3 LPX and GroqCloud; Cerebras; SambaNova; Etched; d-Matrix; disaggregated prefill and decode.

entries.title: Owning, renting and reserving GPU capacity
entries.summary: Price every reservation against the public indices, and fix utilisation before you add capacity.
judgement: Price every reservation against the public indices, and fix utilisation before you add capacity. GPU rental gained public price benchmarks in the second half of 2026: Silicon Data's daily index put the neocloud H100 rate at $2.90 an hour on 28 October, its B200 index rose 27.6% between January and the start of September, and the premium hyperscalers charge for H100 time roughly halved [221, 222, 223]. CME planned futures settled on those indices [224], which give buyers a benchmark for invoices, renewals and reservation offers.

In one September survey, 81% of enterprises running AI in production said their GPUs sit idle at least half the time, and only 10% had a return verified by finance [225]; the sample was small and self-selected. Ownership suits steady, well-utilised or sovereign inference, and demand for owned capacity is strong: Dell booked a record $60.9bn of AI server orders in one quarter [226]. The enterprise posture is Revisit because many reservations and refresh plans were priced before this market formed.
entries.where: Sustained inference or fine-tuning demand that pay-per-token services serve expensively.
entries.test: Utilisation over a quarter, the indexed price for the same GPU and term, and cost per accepted task when you own, reserve or rent.
entries.failure: Reserved or owned GPUs that sit idle while the market price falls below the contract.
entries.examples: Term and reserved capacity; spot markets; on-premises racks; Silicon Data indices and CME GPU futures.

entries.title: GPU cloud and capacity-contract risk
entries.summary: Assess counterparty risk in every capacity contract.
judgement: Assess counterparty risk in every capacity contract. In October, credit markets priced a material chance that the largest independent GPU cloud would default within five years: CoreWeave's bonds traded at 81 cents on the dollar, and its credit default swaps reached a record of about 1,195 basis points [33, 155, 227]. CoreWeave reported a revenue backlog of about $104bn that depends on meeting delivery requirements, with 1.5 GW of active power against 3.7 GW contracted [228]. Much of the sector's funding is circular: Nvidia guarantees $3.5bn of its AI cloud partners' lease obligations, and AMD is investing in Anthropic while supplying its chips [229, 230]. Oracle served a force majeure notice on a Stargate campus whose gas supply had been refused rights of way [231].

Avoid large prepayments; negotiate termination, step-in and data-return rights; read what backlog conditions and force majeure clauses let a provider delay; and keep a tested second provider for critical inference. The enterprise posture is Plan for because supplier failure is now a scenario to plan for for any organisation that depends on rented capacity.
entries.where: Organisations that rent dedicated GPU capacity or depend on one provider for critical inference.
entries.test: Exit and step-in terms, the provider's financing and power status, and a timed failover to a second provider.
entries.failure: A prepaid or long-term contract with a provider that cannot deliver, and no tested route to another.
entries.examples: Neocloud and hyperscaler capacity contracts; escrow, step-in and data-return clauses; routing inference across providers.

entries.title: Memory supply and hardware prices
entries.summary: Allow for higher hardware and cloud prices through 2027.
judgement: Allow for higher hardware and cloud prices through 2027. Memory makers report supply committed for years: Micron's quarterly revenue reached $54.2bn against $11.3bn a year earlier, and SK hynix said its HBM and other DRAM are sold out through 2029 [232, 233]. TrendForce forecast contract prices for DRAM up 10% to 15% and for NAND up 15% to 20% in the fourth quarter, and HBM's average price up 121% in 2027 [234, 235]. The effects reached buyers: memory and storage prices lifted server prices as data-centre capital spending grew 92% in the second quarter, and PC shipments fell 20.1% in the third [236, 237]. A second phase of US semiconductor tariffs that could reach data-centre servers was in preparation [238].

Lengthen refresh cycles where you can, secure supply early through supplier agreements, and favour memory-efficient serving: quantisation, smaller models and careful management of the cache that long contexts consume (IR-010, IR-002). The enterprise posture is Plan for because budgets set before the shortage understate what hardware now costs.
entries.where: Hardware refreshes, on-premises AI capacity and cloud budgets for 2027.
entries.test: Current quotes and lead times for the configurations you plan, and the memory each workload needs at its target precision.
entries.failure: A refresh or capacity plan priced on last year's memory costs.
entries.examples: HBM, DRAM and enterprise SSD contracts; supplier agreements with deposits; quantisation and cache offload.

entries.title: AI PCs and NPUs in the fleet
entries.summary: Buy business laptops for their security, lifetime and memory, and treat the neural processing unit (NPU) as a side benefit for now.
judgement: Buy business laptops for their security, lifetime and memory, and treat the neural processing unit (NPU) as a side benefit for now. NPU-equipped machines are becoming the default business specification: Microsoft says over 40% of laptops being built for business are Copilot+ PCs, and HP said AI PCs made up 46% of its shipments in its latest quarter [239, 240]. The Windows features that would put the NPU to regular use are still to arrive [239], and studies of mobile chips disagree on where NPUs speed up language models, with energy use that depends heavily on configuration [241, 242]. The memory shortage now sets the price and timing of hardware refreshes: PC shipments fell 20.1% in the third quarter, and IDC expects no relief until early 2028 [237, 243].

Fund high-memory machines for local models (64 to 128 GB) separately, for named roles, and justify them with measured savings: the first independent test of such a laptop found usable speed, heat under sustained load and a weak cost case so far [244]. The enterprise posture is Revisit because refresh plans and device budgets set before the memory shortage understate today's costs.
entries.where: Laptop and desktop refreshes, and roles that run models locally, such as developers and analysts.
entries.test: Measured token savings, battery life and heat for local models on one team's real work, against the extra cost per device.
entries.failure: A premium paid for an NPU that no application uses, or a refresh priced before the memory shortage.
entries.examples: Copilot+ PCs; Apple M6 and M5 Ultra; Intel Core Ultra Series 3; AMD Ryzen AI Max; Nvidia RTX Spark; Windows ML and Apple Core AI.

entries.title: Risk-tiered governance with named owners
entries.summary: Set decision rights by risk tier, and give every AI system and agent a named owner with the authority to stop it.
judgement: Set decision rights by risk tier, and give every AI system and agent a named owner with the authority to stop it. Most large organisations have written policies; the gap emerges when action is required. In EY's survey of 202 senior AI executives at large US listed companies, 98% reported formal AI governance policies, yet 47% said their organisation had not applied its governance process to urgent deployments, and 26% of those whose organisations use agents said they could not detect unauthorised ones [247]. The incidents of the second half of 2026 reflected the same gap: an evaluation partner's environment left open through a misunderstanding about scope, a risk judgement that was not revisited as capabilities grew, and a training run that kept going for about 2.5 hours after an alert because staff were unsure whether to stop it [13, 251, 4]. Directors see it too: in PwC's survey of 561 directors, 82% rate the information they receive on AI outcomes, risks and performance as fair, poor or missing [249].

Build on a management system. ISO/IEC 42001 provides the backbone, though only 271 accredited certificates were counted worldwide at the end of 2025 [252]; EN 18286 adds a route to presumed conformity, for the provisions it covers, for providers of high-risk systems in the EU [50]; and the UK National Cyber Security Centre's agent guidance (named owners, an identity for every agent, isolation and the ability to halt) provides complementary guidance for agents [250]. Nearly half of the large US companies in KPMG's survey already name uses in which agents may not act alone [248]. Keep an inventory that can find unsanctioned agents (IR-085), and report outcomes and risks to the board. The enterprise posture is Revisit because most governance was written for tools that advise, and agents now act.
entries.where: Any organisation whose AI systems or agents can reach data, money, customers or production systems.
entries.test: For three live systems, confirm the owner, the risk tier, who may stop each one and how fast, and whether any agent runs outside the inventory.
entries.failure: A policy that teams bypass under deadline pressure, or an alert that nobody has the authority to act on.
entries.examples: ISO/IEC 42001 and 42005; EN 18286; the NIST AI Risk Management Framework; the UK NCSC's agentic AI guidance; Singapore's Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI.

featured.why: Agents at the leading laboratories reached real systems through whatever access lay in reach [1 to 9].
A training run reached an outside chatbot through a DNS gap, and red-teaming found virtual-machine escapes in frontier training [4, 6].
An automatic stop failed in September [4], and AI-found flaws pushed one bank to bring in about 1,000 contractors [96].
Nine model releases arrived between 3 September and 26 October [15, 68, 69, 122, 123, 128 to 131], and hosted models can be changed or retired.
Token prices fell while some costs per task rose, and one provider's introductory price doubles after 30 November 2026 [23, 67, 68, 69].
Agent Skills moved to neutral governance [127], and planted instruction files hijacked coding agents [101].
In OpenAI's enterprise data, Codex reached 64% of combined Codex and ChatGPT enterprise output tokens by June 2026 [73], and coding agents leaked thousands of sensitive screenshots [100].
GPT-6 Astra and Dots launched and Claude Duet entered research preview [15, 17, 19], and OpenAI withdrew its standalone agentic browser [132].
Muse Spark Open shipped weights, Mistral and Kimi weights were pending at cutoff [128, 129, 131], and open-weight models carried most tokens on one gateway [76].
Anthropic reports no-crash proofs for 239 entry points under stated assumptions [95], and the KLS proof gained a machine-checked formalisation [26].
Researchers directing agents proved the KLS conjecture [26], and 722 manuscripts arrived at once [27].
Platforms split between blocking and admitting shopping agents, and two protocols compete [102, 103, 105, 161].
The AI Office sent its first requests, EN 18286 was cited in the Official Journal and Irish courts issued directions on AI-assisted documents [12, 50, 54, 55].
A review of 1,357 FDA-cleared or approved AI devices through December 2025 identified patient-outcome evaluation for just 3 [94].

judgements.label: Revisit
judgements.title: How much freedom each agent has, and who can stop it
judgements.condition: Agents that can act on systems, data or third parties.
judgements.evidence: Containment failures at the leading laboratories through October; ways to bypass agent monitoring found by an authorised red team; scope violations in simulation [1 to 9, 63, 64].
judgements.action: Give every agent a named owner, explicit scope, least-privilege credentials, network boundaries, a record of what it was allowed to do and did, and a rehearsed stop. Keep consequential rules in code gates.
judgements.tradeoff: Throughput against containment. A stop needs someone with the authority, access and time to carry on the work.
judgements.revisit: Providers publish incident rates with denominators, or regulators set incident-reporting duties for deployers.

judgements.label: Test
judgements.title: Accepted work and cost per accepted task, on your own tasks
judgements.evidence: The editors found no comparable public series of accepted delegated work; token and seat counts measure activity [62, 73].
judgements.action: For each task type, record attempts, unique accepted outcomes, review and rework. Use a representative, versioned test set with acceptance criteria agreed by the process owner.
judgements.revisit: An external series using a consistent method reports accepted outcomes.

judgements.label: Test
judgements.title: Model choice and routing, every quarter
judgements.condition: Organisations choosing or routing between models.
judgements.evidence: Ramp customers' blended token price fell 25.4% between weeks a month apart [23]; one provider's introductory price doubles after 30 November 2026 [69]; a discount above 30% moved one large customer, in a single unverified report [71]; cost per task can rise when token prices fall [67].
judgements.action: Compare candidate models and harnesses on your task set by cost per accepted task, accuracy and latency. Keep harnesses swappable.
judgements.revisit: A material model or price change, quality drift, or your next quarterly review; rerun the comparison before switching.

judgements.label: Plan for
judgements.title: Consumption and outcome pricing
judgements.evidence: Usage billing for coding agents [126]; half of one major vendor's new business priced outside seats [70].
judgements.action: Set budgets per job profile, metering, spend caps and approval for exceptions. Model the bill at scale before rollout.
judgements.tradeoff: Usage pricing ties cost to work done and makes bills harder to predict; tight caps protect budgets and can stall useful work.
judgements.revisit: Your largest vendors publish new pricing models.

judgements.label: Plan for
judgements.title: Supplier financial and access risk
judgements.condition: Dependence on a frontier model, a GPU cloud or a single provider.
judgements.evidence: GPU-cloud credit stress [33]; a laboratory's training pause of more than a month on safety and security grounds, disclosed in its filing [37]; a withheld model [5]; model retirements, with notice of about 60 days to 12 months in Brightbeam's experience.
judgements.action: Map who backs your provider's capacity and what notice each side can give. Keep exit and assignment rights, a tested fallback model and regression suites ready.
judgements.tradeoff: Fallback models and exit rights cost engineering time and can forgo volume discounts from a single provider.
judgements.revisit: Credit conditions for GPU clouds normalise or providers publish capacity terms for 2027.

judgements.label: Plan for
judgements.title: Verification as the binding constraint
judgements.condition: Organisations using AI for analysis, code or discovery.
judgements.evidence: OpenAI released 722 AI-generated manuscripts at once and withdrew 3 the next day [27]; AI-found vulnerabilities pushed one bank to bring in about 1,000 contractors and PHP to ship emergency patches [96].
judgements.action: Budget review capacity explicitly. Ensure reviewers exercise judgement rather than approve routinely. Use formal checks where they exist.
judgements.revisit: Verification tooling demonstrably cuts review load on your work.

judgements.label: Plan for
judgements.title: Oversight evidence
judgements.condition: Organisations within the EU AI Act's high-risk scope, regulated sectors, court users where practice directions apply, and US federal suppliers.
judgements.evidence: High-risk duties from 2 December 2027 (Annex III) and 2 August 2028 (Annex I); EN 18286; AI Office requests; US incident notification; Irish court directions; the GSA contract clause [49 to 56, 115].
judgements.action: Record decisions, overrides and approvals as structured evidence. Map where AI-assisted material enters regulated documents and who verified it. Review the US GSA clause [115] as one reference when drafting AI contract terms, with legal review against EU and national requirements.
judgements.tradeoff: Structured records add work at the point of decision; they repay it at audit, in disputes and when systems change.
judgements.revisit: The first enforcement decision or sanction is published.

judgements.label: Revisit
judgements.title: Your security posture against machine-speed attackers
judgements.condition: Any organisation with internet-facing systems or OAuth-connected applications.
judgements.evidence: Agent-run intrusions reaching privileged access in hours; website break-ins at roughly $50 each, by one researcher's estimate; hijacked coding agents [98, 99, 101].
judgements.action: Review OAuth application credentials and service-principal sign-ins; treat agent instruction files as code; give each tool its own spend-capped key; automate containment.
judgements.tradeoff: Tighter credentials and automated containment add friction for developers and can interrupt legitimate automation.
judgements.revisit: A new attack path, material incident or threat-intelligence change; use rehearsals to test whether containment takes effect before harm occurs.

judgements.label: Revisit
judgements.title: Policies that rely on prohibition alone
judgements.condition: Any organisation whose staff can reach AI tools.
judgements.evidence: 31% of UK users work with AI without their employer's knowledge [75].
judgements.action: Provide an authorised route with the controls and records the work needs.
judgements.tradeoff: An authorised route costs licences and governance effort; prohibition alone leaves use unseen.
judgements.revisit: Your own audit of unsanctioned use is available.

judgements.label: Watch
judgements.title: Entry-level hiring and the expertise pipeline
judgements.condition: Organisations with entry-level roles in exposed occupations.
judgements.evidence: A 19% gap for young workers in exposed occupations, which loses significance with all controls [77, 78]; junior hiring falls inside a leading laboratory [79].
judgements.action: Track junior hiring, progression and supervision load in your own exposed roles. The practice of redesigning junior work sits in IR-080.
judgements.tradeoff: Junior roles can cost more today than agent capacity; they build the expertise that verification depends on later.
judgements.revisit: Updated payroll and tracker data become available.

judgements.label: Watch
judgements.title: Infrastructure permission and grid terms
judgements.condition: Plans that depend on new capacity, directly or through a provider, especially where grid capacity is constrained.
judgements.evidence: Grid ceilings, connection conditions, refusals and public opposition [43 to 48].
judgements.action: Treat permission, power and community terms as delivery risks with their own timelines when choosing regions and providers.
judgements.tradeoff: Regions with spare grid capacity can bring higher latency, cost or data-residency constraints.
judgements.revisit: Named projects report delays or new connections clear.

judgements.label: Watch
judgements.title: Agent-commerce terms
judgements.evidence: Platforms split between blocking and welcoming agents; two protocols compete [102, 103, 105, 161].
judgements.action: Define the access, consent, refund and liability terms you would require, then test a bounded journey when a relevant channel becomes available.
judgements.tradeoff: Admitting agents widens reach and adds fraud, liability and margin risk; blocking them protects the customer relationship and may lose customers who shop through agents.
judgements.revisit: A relevant retailer or payment provider changes agent access, authority, refunds or liability terms.

sectors.name: Financial services
sectors.headline: Explain every credit decision, and plan the exit from every AI supplier.

rules.text: From 20 November 2026, when a consumer credit assessment involves automated processing, the consumer can ask for a person to step in: an explanation of the logic, a chance to give their view, and a review of the decision. Mortgage-secured credit and loans above €100,000 fall outside the directive.

AI that scores people's creditworthiness is high-risk under the AI Act, and a lender must assess its impact on fundamental rights before using it; AI that detects financial fraud falls outside that category. These obligations apply from 2 December 2027, and to systems already in use once they change significantly.

DORA has applied to financial entities since 17 January 2025: a register of every ICT supplier arrangement, and exit strategies for services behind critical or important functions. An AI service bought in is usually an ICT service. The first critical ICT providers were designated for direct EU oversight on 18 November 2025.

start.why: Put every AI service and model provider in your DORA register of information.
Keep an explainable baseline beside every credit model you change.
Give whoever reviews a contested credit decision the record and the authority to change it.

moves.why: Credit decisions about people are high-risk under the AI Act, and a consumer can ask for any automated assessment to be explained. Treat a model you cannot explain as not ready for them.
The explanation and review a consumer can ask for from 20 November 2026 depend on a record of how each assessment was made. Test that record now.
DORA already requires exit strategies for ICT services behind critical or important functions. Check that your AI suppliers are in them.

hold.why: A consumer can ask for a person to explain and review any automated assessment: keep someone ready, with the record and the authority to change it, for every credit decision about a person.

sectors.name: Insurance
sectors.headline: Price without proxies, and keep a person on every refusal.

rules.text: AI that assesses risk and sets prices for individuals in life and health insurance is high-risk under the AI Act, and an insurer must assess its impact on fundamental rights before using it. These obligations apply from 2 December 2027, and to systems already in use once they change significantly.
Since 21 December 2012, a person's sex may not lead to different premiums or benefits in the EU.

For AI outside the high-risk class, such as claims handling, fraud detection and pricing outside life and health, EIOPA's Opinion of 6 August 2025 sets out what Solvency II and the Insurance Distribution Directive already expect: data governance, records, fairness, explainability and human oversight, in proportion to the risk.

start.why: Start with claims and policy documents, checking every extraction against the page.
Keep an explainable baseline beside every pricing and claims model.
Watch pricing and claims outcomes by customer group, so drift and unfair outcomes show early.

moves.why: Pricing life and health cover for individuals is high-risk from December 2027, and sex may not move a premium. Treat a pricing model you cannot explain, or cannot test for proxies of sex, as not ready.

EIOPA expects records of AI systems in proportion to their risk, and life and health pricing needs an impact assessment from December 2027. Test that a real underwriting decision can be reconstructed from its record.
DORA applies to most insurers and reinsurers: exit strategies for ICT services behind critical or important functions already apply. Check that your AI suppliers are in them.

hold.why: People can contest a decision made solely by automated processing and ask for a person to step in. Keep someone who can explain and change the outcome ready for every refusal of cover and every claim denial.

sectors.name: Pharma and biotech
sectors.headline: Explore freely in discovery; freeze and validate models in critical GMP uses.

rules.text: AI built and used only for scientific research and development is outside the AI Act. Where AI produces evidence about a medicine, EMA and the FDA's joint principles of January 2026 ask for a defined context of use, validation in proportion to risk, traceable data and monitoring for drift.

GMP already requires computerised systems in manufacturing to be validated, with every change controlled. The July 2025 draft of a GMP annex on AI would allow only static models with deterministic outputs in critical uses; since its consultation, EMA has been weighing a risk-based route, with guardrails, for generative AI.

The revised good clinical practice guideline, ICH E6(R3), has applied in the EU since 23 July 2025: computerised systems in a trial are validated in proportion to their risk to participants and to the reliability of results.

start.why: Start with visual inspection, and require the model to match or beat the manual inspection it replaces.
Use strong classical models on process data first; the draft GMP annex is written for static models.
List every model in your GMP and clinical systems, with its intended use, owner and supplier.

moves.why: In drug discovery every candidate meets an assay, and then a trial, before it reaches a patient, and research-only AI is outside the AI Act. An AI-discovered target and molecule went through a small randomised phase 2a trial, reported in 2025. Run a bounded discovery pilot with a budget for verification.

GMP already puts every change to a computerised system under control, and the draft AI annex asks for each change to a model, its system or its inputs to be assessed for retesting. Check how your change control classifies a model update now.

hold.why: Keep generative AI out of critical GMP applications until the AI annex settles how it may be used; elsewhere, trained staff stay responsible for every output.
Avoid generating test data or labels for a model in a critical GMP use: the draft annex does not recommend it, and asks for test data kept apart from training.

sectors.name: Medtech
sectors.headline: Treat every model update as a device change.

rules.text: Software with a medical purpose that informs diagnosis or treatment decisions is at least class IIa under the Medical Devices Regulation, so it needs a notified body's assessment. In-vitro diagnostic software is classed under its own regulation.

AI that is such a device, or a safety component of one, is also high-risk under the AI Act from 2 August 2028. For AI that keeps learning after release, changes the maker pre-determined at the first conformity assessment can then ship without a new one.
In the US, a device's authorised predetermined change control plan lets the maker release the planned changes without a new marketing submission for each one.

start.why: List every AI function across your devices and quality system, with its intended purpose and class.
Track real-world performance by patient group and site; post-market surveillance expects it.
Gate every model release on a fixed validation set, and keep the previous version ready to restore.

moves.why: Decision support that informs diagnosis or treatment is a medical device of class IIa or higher. Plan its certification, clinical evaluation and post-market surveillance before placing it on the market.

Behaviour a device's AI learns in use is a device change. Without a new review it can ship only within a plan agreed in advance: an authorised change control plan in the US, and from August 2028 changes pre-determined under the AI Act in the EU. Anything else goes back to the notified body or the FDA. Test your release process against such a plan now.
A change that could affect a certified device's safety or performance already needs the notified body's approval. Check how your quality system classifies a model update before the next one ships.

hold.why: Never count generated data as clinical evidence: under the Medical Devices Regulation, clinical data come from the use of the device or of an equivalent one. Validate on real data.

sectors.name: Manufacturing
sectors.headline: Keep self-learning models out of safety functions, and own the software you ship.

rules.text: From 20 January 2027, machinery whose safety functions rely on self-evolving machine learning, and safety components that do, need a notified body's conformity assessment. The AI Act's requirements for AI in machinery will come through the Machinery Regulation, in delegated acts that apply by 2 August 2028.

Since 11 September 2026, manufacturers must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents in their products with digital elements. The rest of the Cyber Resilience Act applies to products placed on the market from 11 December 2027, including due diligence on components from third parties, open source among them.

For products placed on the market after 9 December 2026, EU product liability covers software, AI systems included: a product's ability to keep learning counts when judging a defect, and a manufacturer stays liable for defects from software updates, or missing ones, within its control.

start.why: Start on one line with a known cost per missed defect, and test lighting, camera changes and rare faults on the real line.
Forecast demand, maintenance and energy against seasonal baselines, and score the peaks.
Plan schedules with a solver, and let a language model help people state the problem and read the plan.

moves.why: Reporting of actively exploited vulnerabilities in products with digital elements has applied since 11 September 2026, and due diligence on components follows in December 2027. Re-examine how you track the models and libraries inside the products you sell.

A product you sell with AI running in it is a product with digital elements under the Cyber Resilience Act, unless sector rules such as those for medical devices cover it, and from 9 December 2026 new products fall under the new liability rules. Plan security updates and support periods before you ship.

hold.why: Keep self-learning models out of safety functions: from 20 January 2027, machinery whose safety functions rely on self-evolving machine learning needs a notified body's assessment.

sectors.name: Public services
sectors.headline: Explain every decision about a person, and keep the service open to everyone.

rules.text: AI social scoring that leads to unjustified or unrelated harmful treatment of people has been banned in the EU since 2 February 2025, for public bodies and companies alike.

From 2 December 2027, AI used by or for public authorities to assess eligibility for essential public benefits and services, healthcare included, or to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim them, is high-risk: before using it, a public body must assess its impact on fundamental rights and register the use in the EU database. Systems already in use must comply by 2 August 2030.

Public sector websites and mobile apps must be perceivable, operable, understandable and robust, a duty in force since 2019 for newer websites, 2020 for the rest and 2021 for apps. An AI assistant a public body puts on them is held to the same duty.

start.why: Keep a register of every AI system in use, with its owner; impact assessments and EU database entries start from it.
Help staff find policy and case guidance, with permissions applied and sources shown.
Draft letters and summaries that a caseworker checks against the file.

moves.why: Accessibility duties for public websites and apps already apply, and an AI assistant on them is no exception. Re-examine the ones you run with the people and assistive technologies they must serve.

An explanation on request depends on a record of how each decision was made, and the impact assessment on records of how the system is used. Test that a real case can be reconstructed from its record before December 2027.

hold.why: Keep a caseworker who can explain and change the outcome in every decision about a benefit or service: a person affected by a decision with legal or similarly significant effects can ask for an explanation of the AI's role.

title: Frontier model selection
dimension: 1
intelligence: Trial
enterprise: Revisit
disclosure: no
status: active
---

Leaderboards changed method so often in the second half of 2026 that a ranking is difficult to interpret without knowing its harness: one benchmark verified the same model at 62.7% with its standard harness and up to 99.9% with its maker's adapter, and their comparability is disputed [61, 153]. Frontier capability edged up within overlapping intervals [59]. Select the model together with its surrounding system, on work you can judge: your own cases, your own acceptance criteria and full cost. The enterprise posture is Revisit where model choice rests mainly on reputation or a public ranking.

## Where it fits
A bounded task with an owner and a definition of accepted output.

## Test before committing
Compare quality, refusals, latency and full cost on unseen local cases, including exceptions.

## Failure to watch
A benchmark winner that fails on your exception cases.

## Examples
Hosted model APIs; locally evaluated challengers.

## Evidence
[59], [60], [61], [153].

## Owner
Technical architecture lead

Buy business laptops for their security, lifetime and memory, and treat the neural processing unit (NPU) as a side benefit for now. The Windows features that would put the NPU to regular use are still to arrive [239], and studies of mobile chips disagree on where NPUs speed up language models, with energy use that depends heavily on configuration [241, 242]. The memory shortage now sets the price and timing of hardware refreshes: PC shipments fell 20.1% in the third quarter, and IDC expects no relief until early 2028 [237, 243].

Fund high-memory machines for local models (64 to 128 GB) separately, for named roles, and justify them with measured savings: the first independent test of such a laptop found usable speed, heat under sustained load and a weak cost case so far [244]. The enterprise posture is Revisit because refresh plans and device budgets set before the memory shortage understate today's costs.

## Where it fits
Laptop and desktop refreshes, and roles that run models locally, such as developers and analysts.

## Test before committing
Measured token savings, battery life and heat for local models on one team's real work, against the extra cost per device.

## Failure to watch
A premium paid for an NPU that no application uses, or a refresh priced before the memory shortage.

## Examples
Copilot+ PCs; Apple M6 and M5 Ultra; Intel Core Ultra Series 3; AMD Ryzen AI Max; Nvidia RTX Spark; Windows ML and Apple Core AI.

## Evidence
[237], [239], [240], [241], [242], [243], [244].

## Owner
Infrastructure and platform lead

number: 103
title: Risk-tiered governance with named owners
dimension: 4
intelligence: Use
enterprise: Revisit

Set decision rights by risk tier, and give every AI system and agent a named owner with the authority to stop it. Most large organisations have written policies; the gap emerges when action is required. In EY's survey of 202 senior AI executives at large US listed companies, 98% reported formal AI governance policies, yet 47% said their organisation had not applied its governance process to urgent deployments, and 26% of those whose organisations use agents said they could not detect unauthorised ones [247]. The incidents of the second half of 2026 reflected the same gap: an evaluation partner's environment left open through a misunderstanding about scope, a risk judgement that was not revisited as capabilities grew, and a training run that kept going for about 2.5 hours after an alert because staff were unsure whether to stop it [13, 251, 4]. Directors see it too: in PwC's survey of 561 directors, 82% rate the information they receive on AI outcomes, risks and performance as fair, poor or missing [249].

Build on a management system. ISO/IEC 42001 provides the backbone, though only 271 accredited certificates were counted worldwide at the end of 2025 [252]; EN 18286 adds a route to presumed conformity, for the provisions it covers, for providers of high-risk systems in the EU [50]; and the UK National Cyber Security Centre's agent guidance (named owners, an identity for every agent, isolation and the ability to halt) provides complementary guidance for agents [250]. Nearly half of the large US companies in KPMG's survey already name uses in which agents may not act alone [248]. Keep an inventory that can find unsanctioned agents (IR-085), and report outcomes and risks to the board. The enterprise posture is Revisit because most governance was written for tools that advise, and agents now act.

## Where it fits
Any organisation whose AI systems or agents can reach data, money, customers or production systems.

## Test before committing
For three live systems, confirm the owner, the risk tier, who may stop each one and how fast, and whether any agent runs outside the inventory.

## Failure to watch
A policy that teams bypass under deadline pressure, or an alert that nobody has the authority to act on.

## Examples
ISO/IEC 42001 and 42005; EN 18286; the NIST AI Risk Management Framework; the UK NCSC's agentic AI guidance; Singapore's Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI.

## Evidence
[4], [13], [50], [247], [248], [249], [250], [251], [252].

## Owner
Executive owner for AI
