1.name: Models and inference
1.covers: Choosing, sizing, routing, hosting and serving models
1.intro: The model is still the engine, and the decisions that determine whether one works in an organisation now sit around it: how to choose it, size it, route work to it, host it and serve it. Nine major model releases arrived between 3 September and 26 October 2026 [15, 68, 69, 122, 123, 128 to 131], and token prices moved by double digits within weeks [23]. Model choice has become a recurring decision. Treat models as replaceable parts behind stable task contracts, and treat the ability to evaluate and replace them as the lasting asset (IR-049, IR-087).
1.question: Which model, sized and served how, for each task?
1.description: How to choose, size, route, host and serve models. Model choice became a recurring decision in 2026, so this dimension treats models as replaceable parts behind stable task contracts, with the ability to evaluate and replace them as the lasting asset.
implications: Revisit model choices made on reputation or a public ranking, and choose on your own exam (IR-001, IR-049).
Test routing, caching, structured outputs and small models; each cuts cost once your exam confirms the quality (IR-009, IR-011, IR-007, IR-002).
Watch self-hosting and advanced serving optimisations until your volume and skills justify them (IR-003, IR-010, IR-012).

2.name: Knowledge, context and expertise
2.covers: Permissions, retrieval, parsing, graphs, memory, expertise and tacit knowledge, provenance and deletion
2.intro: In Brightbeam's practitioner experience, recurring failures involve what the model was given to read: the wrong version, a document the user should never have seen, a summary that dropped the exception, a memory nobody owns. Knowledge work is where AI earns its value, and context engineering strongly influences the outcome. Retrieve with the user's permissions, keep provenance to the passage, treat what enters the prompt as a versioned decision, and decide who owns an agent's memory before agents start keeping one. Persistent personal agents launched in the second half of 2026 make memory ownership a present question [17, 19, 20]. Expertise belongs here too: the judgement of experienced people, recorded with its conditions and checked before others rely on it, often provides context needed for a sound answer (IR-020).
2.question: What does the model see, and who is allowed to see it?
2.description: Everything a model is given to read and remember: retrieval with the user's permissions, parsed documents, memory, provenance, and the judgement of experienced people. These sit together because most failures in knowledge work begin with the wrong context, and expertise is the context that documents leave out.
implications: Revisit any assistant that retrieves without the user's permissions or cites without provenance (IR-013, IR-021).
Test the retrieval stack and the capture of expert judgement on your own documents and cases (IR-014, IR-015, IR-016, IR-020).
Plan for agent memory with owners and expiry, and for corrections and deletions that reach every copy (IR-019, IR-024).

3.name: Agents and workflow
3.covers: Bounded agents, deterministic workflows, durable execution, tool and agent protocols, computer use, approval and coding agents
3.intro: Agents moved from answering to doing in the second half of 2026: computer-use models, persistent personal agents and coding agents now take on whole tasks [15, 17, 19]. In Brightbeam's experience, the projects that work run few agents, with clear limits, identities, budgets and records. Start with a deterministic workflow that calls a model where judgement is needed, then a bounded single agent with a stopping condition, and add more agents only when a measured division of labour pays for the coordination. Put a person where actions are consequential, and give that person the information, time and authority to stop the work.
3.question: How much freedom should software have, and how is it stopped?
3.description: How work is delegated to software that acts: deterministic workflows, bounded agents, durable execution, tool protocols, computer use and coding agents. These sit together because each design choice sets how much freedom the software has and how a person can stop it.
implications: Revisit agent designs that skip a deterministic workflow, human takeover or a sandbox; all three are ready now (IR-026, IR-032, IR-034).
Test bounded single agents, durable execution, MCP tools and coding agents on measured work (IR-025, IR-027, IR-028, IR-035).
Plan for computer-use agents arriving through vendors, and hold back open-ended autonomy (IR-031, IR-036).

4.name: Assurance, security and governance
4.covers: Decision rights and accountable owners, regulatory readiness, identity, prompt injection, data protection, independent testing, red-teaming, supply chain, oversight records, incidents and formal proof
4.intro: The defining incidents of the second half of 2026 were containment failures [1 to 9], and attackers adopted agents too [98, 99]. Assurance for AI starts in the environment: identities scoped to the task, secrets kept out of what the model can see, tests the agent cannot reach, and a stop that someone has rehearsed. It ends in evidence: records that let a reviewer reconstruct a decision, and assurance cases that trace each claim to an artefact. Several of these practices are ready today, and the gap lies in how widely organisations apply them. Governance sits here as well: decision rights set by risk tier, a named owner with the authority to stop each system, and a dated view of what each obligation requires (IR-103, IR-092).
4.question: Who may act, who can stop it, and what proves it?
4.description: What makes AI dependable and accountable: identity and least privilege, security testing, incident containment, oversight records, regulation and governance by risk tier. Assurance, security and governance sit together because each depends on knowing who may act, who can stop it and what evidence shows it.
implications: Revisit agent identities, independent grading, the stop and governance by risk tier; these practices are ready and often missing (IR-037, IR-040, IR-045, IR-103).
Test prompt-injection resilience, data-loss controls and red-teaming on your own systems (IR-038, IR-039, IR-041).
Plan for supply-chain verification, oversight records, conformance evidence and regulatory readiness as obligations take effect (IR-042, IR-043, IR-047, IR-092).

5.name: Evaluation and learning
5.covers: Owned exams, system evaluation, calibrated judges, accepted work and full cost, drift, staged release, adaptation and governed learning
5.intro: Accuracy matters when the test represents the work you intend to delegate. In the second half of 2026, leaderboards changed method within weeks, one harness moved a model's score by tens of points, and agents took planted shortcuts when a test rewarded them [61, 84]. Evaluation is therefore an organisational asset: a frozen, versioned examination of the work you intend to delegate, a measure of accepted work and its full cost, and a way to release, observe and recall changes, including changes that agents learn for themselves. These practices let an organisation change models and harnesses safely, which is where the lasting advantage sits.
5.question: How do you know it works, and how does it improve safely?
5.description: How an organisation measures AI on its own work and improves it safely: owned exams, system evaluation, calibrated judges, accepted work and full cost, staged release and governed learning. These sit together because each lets you change models and harnesses without losing control of quality.
implications: Revisit any delegation that rests on vendor benchmarks, and build an owned exam for the work first (IR-049).
Test full-system evaluation, accepted work at full cost, and staged releases (IR-050, IR-052, IR-054).
Plan for governed learning releases, and keep self-modifying production agents on watch (IR-058, IR-060).

6.name: Prediction, science and physical AI
6.covers: Classical and foundation prediction, causal inference, optimisation, vision, graphs, simulation, discovery and robotics
6.intro: Choose the right instrument for each decision. Generation is one capability among several: classification, forecasting, optimisation, graph reasoning, simulation and causal inference each have mature methods that often beat a language model on their own ground, with the language model as interface and orchestrator. This dimension also holds the most visible discoveries of the second half of 2026, made by people directing AI under careful limits [25, 26, 90], and the physical frontier, where the editors counsel patience: harm in the physical world cannot be rolled back like a software release.
6.question: Which instrument fits the decision, beyond a language model?
6.description: AI beyond language: predictive models for tables and time series, causal inference, optimisation, computer vision, simulation, scientific discovery and robots. These sit together because they model the statistical and physical world and are judged against measurement; on their own ground they often beat a general language model, which serves as their interface.
implications: Revisit generative models used for prediction problems, where strong classical baselines often win (IR-061).
Test tabular and time-series foundation models, optimisation and inspection vision against those baselines (IR-062, IR-063, IR-065, IR-066).
Plan review capacity for AI-assisted discovery, and watch robotics and physical autonomy, where harm cannot be rolled back (IR-069, IR-071, IR-072).

7.name: Work, products and people
7.covers: Assistance, service, search, process, expert decision support, media, apprenticeship, literacy, inclusion and commerce
7.intro: This dimension covers how AI changes people's work and the services they deliver. The evidence is uneven. Before the period, firms used AI to supplement, substitute and add tasks at once, and most reported no change in employment [83]; in the second half of 2026, 60% of respondents to one survey said their workload rose [24]; and the most visible labour signal, an estimate that loses significance with all controls, sits in entry-level hiring [77, 78]. Start with reviewable work where people can judge both the content and its evidence, judge services by the customer and staff outcome, keep the routes by which juniors become experts, and design services for everyone who must use them, in every language they need.
7.question: What changes for people, their work and their customers?
7.description: How AI changes people's work and the services they deliver: drafting, customer service, search, expert decision support, media, learning, literacy, accessibility and commerce. These sit together because value appears in work that people accept and in outcomes for customers and staff.
implications: Revisit deflection targets, undisclosed generated media, prohibition-only policies and organisation-wide productivity claims (IR-075, IR-079, IR-081, IR-084).
Test drafting, service copilots, search and expert decision support where people can judge the result (IR-073, IR-074, IR-076, IR-078).
Plan for the routes by which juniors become experts when AI does the routine work (IR-080).

8.name: Operations, economics and sovereignty
8.covers: Inventory, traces, releases, cost, spend controls, resilience, sovereignty, validated change and national evidence
8.intro: Running intelligence in live work is an operating discipline. In the second half of 2026, models were released and retired, the blended token price Ramp's customers paid fell by about a quarter in a month, and one provider set its introductory price to double after 30 November [23, 69]. The organisations that cope know what they run and who owns it, release model changes through evaluation gates, measure cost against accepted work, bound spending at the system boundary, rehearse supplier exit, and validate changes where regulation requires it. Many of its entries sit in the Prepare ring: readiness here is urgent while several technologies are still maturing.
8.question: Can you run it, pay for it and leave it?
8.description: Running AI in live work: inventory, traces, releases, cost and spend controls, resilience, sovereignty and validated change. These sit together because each keeps a live system known, affordable and replaceable.
implications: Revisit your AI inventory, and sovereignty decisions that stop at the hosting region (IR-085, IR-091).
Test purposeful tracing and cost per accepted task (IR-086, IR-088).
Plan for evaluation-gated releases, spend limits, supplier exit, validated change and continuous operation (IR-087, IR-089, IR-090, IR-093, IR-096).

9.name: Compute and hardware
9.covers: Accelerators and portability, inference-specialised chips, owning and renting capacity, GPU cloud contracts, memory and supply, power and location, AI PCs, NPUs and edge devices
9.intro: Hardware sets the price, the speed and the availability of everything above it. In the second half of 2026 a second accelerator family became practical for inference, specialised chips made some models several times faster, GPU rental gained public price benchmarks with public daily indices, the largest independent GPU cloud's credit came under stress, and a memory shortage raised server prices and cut PC shipments by a fifth [208, 215, 221, 33, 236, 237]. Most organisations will rent their compute; the decisions that matter are what they commit to, with whom, and how portable their serving stays. Keep models portable across accelerators, price every reservation against the indices, assess counterparty risk in capacity contracts, and buy devices for their memory and their lifetime. Power, permission and location decide where capacity can go (IR-094).
9.question: Where does it run, on what, and at what price and risk?
9.description: The machines underneath: accelerators and their software, inference-specialised chips, owned and rented capacity, GPU cloud contracts, memory supply, power and location, and the PCs and edge devices that run models locally. These sit together because hardware sets the price, the speed and the availability of everything above it.
implications: Revisit GPU reservations against the public price indices, and device budgets set before the memory shortage (IR-099, IR-102).
Test a second accelerator, fast inference services and on-device models on your own workloads (IR-097, IR-098, IR-070).
Plan for supplier failure and higher hardware prices through 2027, and watch power and permission where capacity is built (IR-100, IR-101, IR-094).

financial-services.name: Financial services
financial-services.headline: Explain every credit decision, and plan the exit from every AI supplier.

rules.text: From 20 November 2026, when a consumer credit assessment involves automated processing, the consumer can ask for a person to step in: an explanation of the logic, a chance to give their view, and a review of the decision. Mortgage-secured credit and loans above €100,000 fall outside the directive.

AI that scores people's creditworthiness is high-risk under the AI Act, and a lender must assess its impact on fundamental rights before using it; AI that detects financial fraud falls outside that category. These obligations apply from 2 December 2027, and to systems already in use once they change significantly.

DORA has applied to financial entities since 17 January 2025: a register of every ICT supplier arrangement, and exit strategies for services behind critical or important functions. An AI service bought in is usually an ICT service. The first critical ICT providers were designated for direct EU oversight on 18 November 2025.

start.why: Put every AI service and model provider in your DORA register of information.
Keep an explainable baseline beside every credit model you change.
Give whoever reviews a contested credit decision the record and the authority to change it.

moves.why: Credit decisions about people are high-risk under the AI Act, and a consumer can ask for any automated assessment to be explained. Treat a model you cannot explain as not ready for them.
The explanation and review a consumer can ask for from 20 November 2026 depend on a record of how each assessment was made. Test that record now.
DORA already requires exit strategies for ICT services behind critical or important functions. Check that your AI suppliers are in them.

hold.why: A consumer can ask for a person to explain and review any automated assessment: keep someone ready, with the record and the authority to change it, for every credit decision about a person.

insurance.name: Insurance
insurance.headline: Price without proxies, and keep a person on every refusal.

rules.text: AI that assesses risk and sets prices for individuals in life and health insurance is high-risk under the AI Act, and an insurer must assess its impact on fundamental rights before using it. These obligations apply from 2 December 2027, and to systems already in use once they change significantly.
Since 21 December 2012, a person's sex may not lead to different premiums or benefits in the EU.

For AI outside the high-risk class, such as claims handling, fraud detection and pricing outside life and health, EIOPA's Opinion of 6 August 2025 sets out what Solvency II and the Insurance Distribution Directive already expect: data governance, records, fairness, explainability and human oversight, in proportion to the risk.

start.why: Start with claims and policy documents, checking every extraction against the page.
Keep an explainable baseline beside every pricing and claims model.
Watch pricing and claims outcomes by customer group, so drift and unfair outcomes show early.

moves.why: Pricing life and health cover for individuals is high-risk from December 2027, and sex may not move a premium. Treat a pricing model you cannot explain, or cannot test for proxies of sex, as not ready.

EIOPA expects records of AI systems in proportion to their risk, and life and health pricing needs an impact assessment from December 2027. Test that a real underwriting decision can be reconstructed from its record.
DORA applies to most insurers and reinsurers: exit strategies for ICT services behind critical or important functions already apply. Check that your AI suppliers are in them.

hold.why: People can contest a decision made solely by automated processing and ask for a person to step in. Keep someone who can explain and change the outcome ready for every refusal of cover and every claim denial.

pharma-and-biotech.name: Pharma and biotech
pharma-and-biotech.headline: Explore freely in discovery; freeze and validate models in critical GMP uses.

rules.text: AI built and used only for scientific research and development is outside the AI Act. Where AI produces evidence about a medicine, EMA and the FDA's joint principles of January 2026 ask for a defined context of use, validation in proportion to risk, traceable data and monitoring for drift.

GMP already requires computerised systems in manufacturing to be validated, with every change controlled. The July 2025 draft of a GMP annex on AI would allow only static models with deterministic outputs in critical uses; since its consultation, EMA has been weighing a risk-based route, with guardrails, for generative AI.

The revised good clinical practice guideline, ICH E6(R3), has applied in the EU since 23 July 2025: computerised systems in a trial are validated in proportion to their risk to participants and to the reliability of results.

start.why: Start with visual inspection, and require the model to match or beat the manual inspection it replaces.
Use strong classical models on process data first; the draft GMP annex is written for static models.
List every model in your GMP and clinical systems, with its intended use, owner and supplier.

moves.why: In drug discovery every candidate meets an assay, and then a trial, before it reaches a patient, and research-only AI is outside the AI Act. An AI-discovered target and molecule went through a small randomised phase 2a trial, reported in 2025. Run a bounded discovery pilot with a budget for verification.

GMP already puts every change to a computerised system under control, and the draft AI annex asks for each change to a model, its system or its inputs to be assessed for retesting. Check how your change control classifies a model update now.

hold.why: Keep generative AI out of critical GMP applications until the AI annex settles how it may be used; elsewhere, trained staff stay responsible for every output.
Avoid generating test data or labels for a model in a critical GMP use: the draft annex does not recommend it, and asks for test data kept apart from training.

medtech.name: Medtech
medtech.headline: Treat every model update as a device change.

rules.text: Software with a medical purpose that informs diagnosis or treatment decisions is at least class IIa under the Medical Devices Regulation, so it needs a notified body's assessment. In-vitro diagnostic software is classed under its own regulation.

AI that is such a device, or a safety component of one, is also high-risk under the AI Act from 2 August 2028. For AI that keeps learning after release, changes the maker pre-determined at the first conformity assessment can then ship without a new one.
In the US, a device's authorised predetermined change control plan lets the maker release the planned changes without a new marketing submission for each one.

start.why: List every AI function across your devices and quality system, with its intended purpose and class.
Track real-world performance by patient group and site; post-market surveillance expects it.
Gate every model release on a fixed validation set, and keep the previous version ready to restore.

moves.why: Decision support that informs diagnosis or treatment is a medical device of class IIa or higher. Plan its certification, clinical evaluation and post-market surveillance before placing it on the market.

Behaviour a device's AI learns in use is a device change. Without a new review it can ship only within a plan agreed in advance: an authorised change control plan in the US, and from August 2028 changes pre-determined under the AI Act in the EU. Anything else goes back to the notified body or the FDA. Test your release process against such a plan now.
A change that could affect a certified device's safety or performance already needs the notified body's approval. Check how your quality system classifies a model update before the next one ships.

hold.why: Never count generated data as clinical evidence: under the Medical Devices Regulation, clinical data come from the use of the device or of an equivalent one. Validate on real data.

manufacturing.name: Manufacturing
manufacturing.headline: Keep self-learning models out of safety functions, and own the software you ship.

rules.text: From 20 January 2027, machinery whose safety functions rely on self-evolving machine learning, and safety components that do, need a notified body's conformity assessment. The AI Act's requirements for AI in machinery will come through the Machinery Regulation, in delegated acts that apply by 2 August 2028.

Since 11 September 2026, manufacturers must report actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents in their products with digital elements. The rest of the Cyber Resilience Act applies to products placed on the market from 11 December 2027, including due diligence on components from third parties, open source among them.

For products placed on the market after 9 December 2026, EU product liability covers software, AI systems included: a product's ability to keep learning counts when judging a defect, and a manufacturer stays liable for defects from software updates, or missing ones, within its control.

start.why: Start on one line with a known cost per missed defect, and test lighting, camera changes and rare faults on the real line.
Forecast demand, maintenance and energy against seasonal baselines, and score the peaks.
Plan schedules with a solver, and let a language model help people state the problem and read the plan.

moves.why: Reporting of actively exploited vulnerabilities in products with digital elements has applied since 11 September 2026, and due diligence on components follows in December 2027. Re-examine how you track the models and libraries inside the products you sell.

A product you sell with AI running in it is a product with digital elements under the Cyber Resilience Act, unless sector rules such as those for medical devices cover it, and from 9 December 2026 new products fall under the new liability rules. Plan security updates and support periods before you ship.

hold.why: Keep self-learning models out of safety functions: from 20 January 2027, machinery whose safety functions rely on self-evolving machine learning needs a notified body's assessment.

public-services.name: Public services
public-services.headline: Explain every decision about a person, and keep the service open to everyone.

rules.text: AI social scoring that leads to unjustified or unrelated harmful treatment of people has been banned in the EU since 2 February 2025, for public bodies and companies alike.

From 2 December 2027, AI used by or for public authorities to assess eligibility for essential public benefits and services, healthcare included, or to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim them, is high-risk: before using it, a public body must assess its impact on fundamental rights and register the use in the EU database. Systems already in use must comply by 2 August 2030.

Public sector websites and mobile apps must be perceivable, operable, understandable and robust, a duty in force since 2019 for newer websites, 2020 for the rest and 2021 for apps. An AI assistant a public body puts on them is held to the same duty.

start.why: Keep a register of every AI system in use, with its owner; impact assessments and EU database entries start from it.
Help staff find policy and case guidance, with permissions applied and sources shown.
Draft letters and summaries that a caseworker checks against the file.

moves.why: Accessibility duties for public websites and apps already apply, and an AI assistant on them is no exception. Re-examine the ones you run with the people and assistive technologies they must serve.

An explanation on request depends on a record of how each decision was made, and the impact assessment on records of how the system is used. Test that a real case can be reconstructed from its record before December 2027.

hold.why: Keep a caseworker who can explain and change the outcome in every decision about a benefit or service: a person affected by a decision with legal or similarly significant effects can ask for an explanation of the AI's role.
